evidence.text: A foot 止 stopping in the right place 一
Pictograph of a foot (止) heading toward a city. Based on the original meaning "go on a military campaign", now written as 征. The meaning later shifted to "power", "rule" (政), and "correct" (正).
是也。从止，一以止。凡正之屬皆从正。

Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *tjeŋ, *tjeŋs): phonetic 丁 (OC *rteːŋ, *teːŋ) + semantic 止 (“foot”) – to go on a long journey. Original form of 征 (OC *tjeŋ, “to go on long campaign”).
Later, 丁 was simplified into a horizontal stroke, as in 旦. Folk etymologies do not recognize 丁. Graphically, the modern version of the character is the reverse of 之.
Sino-Tibetan or area word: “centre; target; first (month); straight; correct”.
Compare Mizo dîng (“to go straight or direct (as person, arrow etc.); to go straight through without breaking the journey; straight; direct”). Matisoff sets up Proto-Sino-Tibetan *m-tjak/ŋ ~ tik/ŋ (“good; very; real; straight”) for this, which includes 正, 直 (OC *dɯɡ, “straight; right”) and 實 (OC *ɦliɡ, “solid; true”).
Additionally, Matisoff has Proto-Sino-Tibetan *t(r)waŋ (“straight; straighten”), whence Chepang धेङ्सा (dʰeŋ-, “straight”), Jingpho ding (“straight”), Tibetan དྲང་པོ (drang po, “straight; correct; upright; just; fair”), Burmese တန်း (tan:, “straight; to head straight for”). Also compare Khmer ទៀង (tiĕng, “accurate; correct; exact; precise; honest”) and Thai ดิ่ง (dìng, “vertically; straight; to plummet”).
Derivatives:
* 征 (OC *tjeŋ, “to go straight > to go on a journey”)
* 政 (OC *tjeŋs, “correct; to govern; government; to determine”)
* 整 (OC *tjeŋʔ, “orderly; to arrange; to dispose”)
For etymology of pronunciation 正 (zhēng) in the month 正月 (zhēngyuè)'s name, see there.
是也。从止，一以止。凡正之屬皆从正。

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database)
evidence.field: 字形、構形分析及甲骨金文用例
evidence.text: The database describes 甲金文 正 as 止 plus 丁; it reports that 丁 is also proposed as a phonetic by Xu Zaiguo and Liu Zhao, while another account treats it as the destination or city and 止 as a foot moving toward it. It calls 正 an early graph for 征 and gives its original sense as travel or a journey, not necessarily warfare. It records oracle-bone examples for military campaign 《合集》6441, first-month dating 《合集》22723, place name 《合集》22246, and a sacrificial name 《合集》14315. It also cites later bronze and Warring States bamboo-slip uses, including 正月, administrative/governmental senses, and 正直. These are reported source interpretations and examples; they do not establish a simple dated semantic path from journey to correct.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 正

evidence.text: The page lists oracle-bone, late Shang and Western Zhou bronze, Warring States, seal, clerical and regular-script evidence, including named inscriptions such as 二祀其卣 (late Shang), 大盂鼎 (early Western Zhou), and later Chu manuscripts. It proposes two parses for early forms: enclosure/city plus foot as an ideographic graph, or 止 plus a filled dot/丁 as phonetic. It describes later reduction of the upper element to a horizontal stroke and records divergent Warring States forms. It interprets early 正 as travel/campaign, with later 正 meanings including central, correct and just; these semantic links are the page's analysis, not directly dated proof of each transition.
evidence.title: 汉字「正」字形演变字源

This is Xu Shen's Han-era graphic analysis, not independent confirmation of the earlier graph's origin. The same page displays examples labeled oracle bone, late Shang/Western Zhou bronze, Warring States, Qin, Western Han and Eastern Han, but does not itself date semantic transitions among those examples.

evidence.field: component analysis, historical forms and reading comparison
evidence.text: Dong Chinese presents 丁 as a sound/iconic component and 止 as the foot component, gives 正 Old Chinese *C.teŋ and *teŋ-s, and gives 丁 *tˤeŋ (with additional forms). It dates displayed forms to oracle script about 1250–1000 BCE, late Shang bronze about 1100 BCE, Shuowen seal script about 100 CE and Eastern Han clerical script 25–220 CE. This account independently supports a phonetic proposal but also treats 丁 iconically as a city wall. The possible phonetic role does not settle the depicted referent, and no reliable original name for a depicted object is established or needed for the component-level phonetic proposal.
evidence.title: 正 — Dong Chinese dictionary

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: The competing early graph parses remain unresolved: the upper form is variously taken as a city/target and as 丁 with a phonetic role; 丁 may also have iconic interpretation. No visually inspected glyph image is claimed here.

The evidence supports early uses including expedition/campaign and first-month dating, but does not provide a secure chronology for the semantic development from travel/campaign to correct, rectifying, central or proper.

The record for first-month 正 is separately associated with Baxter–Sagart *C.teŋ, while correct 正 is *teŋ-s. The precise historical relation between these readings and the character's graphic borrowing history is not demonstrated by the consulted sources.

No independent evidence establishes a recoverable spoken name for any alleged depicted weapon or tool; the researched analysis concerns 丁 as a possible sound component and does not require such an object-name claim.

The supplied local reconstruction rows were checked for 正 only; there was no supplied Baxter–Sagart 丁 row, so no local-row cross-check for 丁 can be reported. The external Baxter–Sagart PDF search result was accessible only as indexed text and direct open failed with HTTP 502.
The official Unihan per-character endpoints for 正, 丁 and 止 were inaccessible. Local kMandarin zhèng is available for 正 only; 丁 and 止 readings remain unchecked.

The early graphic parsing remains disputed: 止 is consistently associated with foot/step, while the upper sign is variously interpreted as city/destination or 丁 used phonically; evidence does not resolve whether both semantic and phonetic functions applied.

The oracle-bone contexts support early expedition/campaign, first-month dating, place-name and sacrifice uses. A dated semantic path from those uses to “correct,” “proper,” “central” or “just” is not established by the inspected evidence.

丁's independent object/referent is not necessary to the component-level phonetic hypothesis. The consulted descriptions do not establish a recoverable original spoken name for a depicted object, so no object-name sound borrowing claim is made.

The supplied local Baxter–Sagart rows for 正 were checked: 正 zhēng / MC tsyeng / OC *C.teŋ (first month) and 正 zhèng / MC tsyengH / OC *teŋ-s (correct). The local 丁 rows give *tˤeŋ for dīng, *tˤreŋ for a distinct zhēng sound-of-beating reading. Similarity of a component reading and one host sense does not establish the historical phonetic analysis; the external table excerpt directly inspected showed 丁 but not the 正 entries.

Official Unihan character-specific pages for U+6B63, U+4E01 and U+6B62 were inaccessible. Local supplied rows report zhèng, dīng and zhǐ respectively; the external official general lookup page only documents how to retrieve those records.

Three reusable modern redraw candidates were sourced from exact Wikimedia description pages. The web viewer did not display their SVG pixels; visual inspection is not claimed. Original-image requests failed in the viewer, so the exact descriptions and declared rights are available but image rendering requires the harness or another SVG-capable client.

The opened Baxter–Sagart PDF did not expose exact 丁 and 正 table rows through its returned text, despite a successful page open; the exact row values here retain local TSV provenance and are not attributed to that inspected external excerpt.
The component phonetic proposal remains disputed because the early upper form can also be interpreted as a destination or enclosure. Similar Baxter–Sagart readings alone do not prove the parse.
No independently recoverable spoken name for an alleged depicted object is established or needed for the 丁 component-level sound proposal; no object-name borrowing claim is made.
The early upper element of 正 remains disputed between a destination/city interpretation and 丁 with a possible phonetic role; phonological resemblance does not decide its graphic identity or function.

The sources report early expedition and first-month uses, as well as place-name and sacrificial-name contexts, but do not establish which was the original sense or a dated semantic transition to ‘correct,’ ‘proper,’ ‘central,’ or ‘just.’

The exact Baxter–Sagart rows are available in the supplied local TSV but were not exposed by the external PDF text inspection in this run; the PDF fetch failed. The distinction between 正’s first-month and ‘correct’ readings is retained.
Official Unihan character-specific records for 丁, 止, and 正 were not opened in this run. Their kMandarin values above are attributed only to supplied local rows, not to inspected Unicode pages.
The two selected Commons glyphs are modern redraws. The web tool did not render their pixels, so the descriptions and proposed captions have not been visually checked here.

items.period: Oracle-script style; file page does not identify a specific inscription date
items.tradition: Oracle-bone script style; modern digital vector redraw
items.caption: An oracle-script-style form of 正 places a boxlike upper element above a footlike lower form. This arrangement fits a reading of a destination with a foot moving toward it, while the upper element is also identified as 丁 with a possible sound role.
items.alt: Black redraw of 正 with a boxlike upper form and a branching, footlike lower form.
items.selection_reason: Shows the early structure relevant to the competing destination and 丁-plus-止 analyses; its shape alone does not resolve them.
items.rights: The file page declares this public domain as a representation of ancient script; attribution is appreciated but not required.

items.period: Bronze-script style; file page does not assign an individual inscription date
items.tradition: Bronze script style; modern digital vector redraw
items.caption: A bronze-script-style form of 正 has a broad upper stroke above an angular lower structure. Bronze examples vary in the upper element, so this drawing illustrates graphic variation without establishing a sequence or settling its interpretation.
items.alt: Black redraw of 正 with a broad top stroke above a tall, angular lower form.
items.selection_reason: Adds a distinct bronze-script form that helps illustrate variation in the upper element; it does not establish chronology.
items.rights: The file page declares this public domain as a representation of ancient script; attribution is appreciated but not required.

limitations.text: The early upper element is interpreted either as a destination or city, or as 丁 with a possible phonetic role; its identity and function remain unresolved. The early uses do not establish a dated development from travel or first-month dating to “correct.”
